text: {place} keeps one light on at this hour and runs the rest on memory.

text: The door of {place} is on the latch and the step has been wet a while.
Two and four is the hour {place} belongs to whoever is still in it.
Cold came in behind me at {place} and took the good chair.
There is grey at the bottom of the sky over {place}, and nothing open yet.
The fog off the river has {place} down to the near kerb and no further.
Gratings are going back at {place} and the first of the day is going to work past me.
{place} at six in the morning is a public room with private hours behind it.
The stairs up to {place} have been swept and the landing has not.
Somebody is always coming out of {place} as I am going in, and never the same somebody.
The block was quiet, every window dark but one. A car idled at the curb with its lights off.
Rain slicked the stoop steps black. A cat crossed under a parked car and didn't look up.
Fog sat low over the row houses, blurring the streetlamps to smears. Somewhere a window sash went down.
The cold cut through, and the block had emptied early because of it. Every stoop light was out but the one over the door.
Not a soul on the block. The moon threw hard shadows off the fire escapes.
The rain had settled into a steady drum on the tin cornices. A dog barked once, twice, then gave it up.
Fog pressed close against the windows, and the street numbers were hard to read past the third house.
Frost had already silvered the iron railings. My own footsteps were the only sound on the block.
The sky was going gray at the edges. A milk bottle sat sweating on a stoop three doors down.
The rain had thinned to a drizzle, and a lamp came on in a kitchen window as I passed. Somebody else was up early too.
The fog was lifting off the rooftops first, leaving the street still socked in. A newspaper lay unclaimed on a stoop, going soft.
The cold had a bite that clear skies bring. Smoke stood straight up from two chimneys on the block.
The block was waking up slow, a door slamming somewhere, a radio coming on upstairs.
Umbrellas were coming out on the stoops, and a boy ran the last block to school with his collar up.
The fog had burned down to a haze at eye level. Somebody's wash hung limp on a line between two windows.
Breath hung in front of every face on the block. A super was already out front, salting the steps.
A last light burned over the shop next to {place}, and the street had the hush that comes after the crowd's thinned. Somebody's radio still played through a cracked window.
Rain beaded on the awnings up and down the block, and the gutter ran fast past {place}. A cab sat at the curb, meter dark.
Fog wrapped the block's lamps into soft yellow rings. {place}'s sign was barely legible from the corner.
The cold had cleared most of the block out early. A last stubborn pair stood outside {place}, not talking.
The block had gone dark storefront by storefront. Only {place} still showed a light through the glass.
Rain ran down the gutter in a steady sheet, and every shop on the block had its grille down but one.
The fog had thickened enough to hide the far corner. {place}'s window was the only light left on the block.
The cold kept the block empty and the glass fogged from inside. {place} was the only warm-looking storefront on the street.
A delivery truck idled outside the grocer's, engine ticking as it cooled. The street was starting to stir before the sun did.
The rain had washed the block clean of last night's crowd. A grate came up two doors from {place}, early and grudging.
Fog hung at window height, thick enough that {place}'s sign showed only its top half. A dog trotted past without slowing, headed somewhere in particular.
Frost furred the awnings along the block. Somebody was already scraping ice off a windshield outside {place}.
The block was in full swing, grilles up, a boy stacking crates outside the grocer's. {place} had its door propped for the morning trade.
Shopkeepers were dragging their awnings out against the drizzle, and the block smelled of wet canvas and fresh coffee.
The fog was thinning off the rooftops, though it still sat low over the gutter. {place} had its lights on against the gray.
Steam rose off the grates along the block, and everyone walking had their collar turned up against it.
The square was near empty, just a few benches holding their regular loiterers. A streetcar rattled through, half lit, nobody aboard.
Rain pocked the empty square, and the fountain basin had gone over its rim. A single cab crossed against the light, wipers going.
Fog softened the square's lamps to a string of pale rings. The benches sat empty, beaded with damp.
The wind came straight across the square with nothing to stop it. Even the pigeons had found somewhere better.
The avenue ran wide and empty under a hard sky. A newspaper turned over once on the pavement and stopped.
The square's lamps threw long reflections down the wet flagstones. Not a soul was out but a sweeper working the gutter.
Fog off the river had swallowed the square's far end whole. A foghorn sounded once, a long way off.
The cold had the square to itself. A newsboy's stack sat unguarded under a lamp, weighted down with a brick.
The first light caught the square's flagstones and made them look scrubbed. A milk wagon crossed at the far end, iron tires loud on the stone.
The rain had slacked to a mist, and the square held a handful of early men with their collars up, going nowhere in particular.
The square was still fogged in, though the shapes of the benches were starting to come clear. A bell somewhere tolled the half hour.
Ice had skinned over the fountain basin in the square. A lone figure crossed fast, breath trailing behind him.
The square had filled in with the morning crowd, pigeons scattering ahead of every third step. The light was flat and full now.
Umbrellas crossed the square from every direction at once, and the flagstones ran with runoff toward the gutters.
The fog had burned off the square but hung on over the river behind it. Traffic was starting up in earnest along the avenue.
The square was busy despite the cold, everybody moving fast to stay warm. Steam curled up off the coffee cart at the corner.
The block outside {place} had gone quiet early, one drunk singing to himself half a block off. My own footsteps sounded too loud for the hour.
A beat cop crossed the square on the diagonal, unhurried, checking doors as he went. Nothing else moved.
Rain ran off {place}'s awning in a steady curtain, and the block smelled of wet brick and spilled beer.
The rain had driven everybody off the square but a man asleep on a bench under yesterday's paper.
The cold kept the block's doors shut tight, and every window along it was fogged from the inside.
The fog muffled the square down to almost nothing, just the click of my own heels on the stone.
The block was still, porch lights out up and down the row. A shade moved once in an upstairs window and settled.
The block had gone dark early, {place}'s window the last one lit on the row.
A lone trolley ground through the square, empty and slow, nobody aboard. The rain kept at it steady.
The grocer's boy was already stacking crates outside, and the block had that early quiet before the trucks start.
Commuters cut across the square at an angle, everyone late for something. The fountain had been turned back on for the day.
The cold had driven even the cats indoors. Nothing moved on the block but a curtain, once, in an upstairs window.
